author: Tertullian
addressee: Christians, especially recent converts and those baptized
occasion: Tertullian writes to persuade Christians that attending public spectacles—circus, theater, stadium, and amphitheater—is incompatible with the faith they professed at baptism. He first answers pagan objections that pleasures do not offend God, then turns to Christians who claim Scripture does not explicitly forbid such entertainments.
argument: Tertullian argues that all public spectacles are rooted in idolatry and therefore belong to the devil, whom Christians renounced at baptism. He traces the origins, titles, apparatus, places, and arts of the games to pagan gods and demon worship. He further argues that the passions aroused by the shows—fury, lust, vanity, cruelty—are contrary to Christian discipline. Since Scripture condemns these vices generally, it implicitly forbids the spectacles that excite them. Christians should replace pagan entertainments with the spiritual pleasures and the coming spectacle of Christ's judgment.

outline.move: Tertullian states his purpose, answers pagan objections that pleasures do not offend God, and establishes that the shows must be judged by their corrupted use, not their divine origin; he then turns to the baptismal renunciation of the devil and his pomp as the chief authority.
He traces the origins, titles, and apparatus of the games to idolatrous worship of pagan gods and the dead.
He examines the places, arts, and patrons of the circus, theater, athletic contests, and gladiatorial games, showing each is consecrated to idols and demons.
He concludes that since all spectacles involve idolatry, Christians must abstain from them entirely, and notes that Scripture's condemnation of worldly desires covers the desire for spectacles.

He argues from the passions each spectacle arouses—fury in the circus, lust in the theater, vanity in the stadium, cruelty in the amphitheater—that they are incompatible with the Holy Spirit and Christian discipline.

He refutes the excuse that God sees all things without being defiled, exposes the inconsistency of pagans who honor yet degrade performers, shows that the arts of the performers themselves are offensive to God, and concludes by returning to the baptismal renunciation as the seal that forbids participation.
He warns that no one can serve both God and the devil, recounts examples of Christians harmed by attending shows, and urges believers to flee gatherings where God is blasphemed.
He contrasts pagan pleasures with Christian joys and the coming spectacle of the Lord's return and final judgment, urging believers to prefer these.

cast.name: Tertullian
cast.who: The author, a Christian teacher in Carthage writing to instruct fellow believers.

cast.name: David
cast.who: The Old Testament king whose psalm is quoted against sitting in the seat of the wicked.

cast.name: Romulus
cast.who: Legendary founder of Rome, credited with instituting the first Roman games.

cast.name: Numa Pompilius
cast.who: Early Roman king who instituted games to Mars and Robigo.

cast.name: Pompey the Great
cast.who: Roman general who built Rome's first permanent theater and dedicated it as a temple of Venus.

cast.name: Timaeus
cast.who: Greek historian cited on the Lydian origin of games in Etruria.

cast.name: Varro
cast.who: Roman scholar cited on the meaning of the word 'ludii'.

cast.name: Piso
cast.who: Roman historian cited on the Tarpeian and Capitoline games.

cast.name: Suetonius Tranquillus
cast.who: Roman historian cited as a source on the founders of the games.

cast.name: Stesichorus
cast.who: Greek poet cited on horses being distributed by Mercury to Castor and Pollux.

cast.name: Erichthonius
cast.who: Legendary son of Minerva and Vulcan, credited with inventing the four-horse chariot.

cast.name: Trochilus
cast.who: Argive credited as an inventor of the chariot, who dedicated it to Juno.

cast.name: Hermateles
cast.who: Writer cited on the obelisk in the circus being dedicated to the Sun.

cast.name: The Apostle
cast.who: Paul, quoted in section 13 on idols being nothing (1 Corinthians 8:4).

scripture: Tertullian quotes the Old Testament from Latin versions influenced by the Septuagint, and the New Testament from Old Latin versions. He cites Psalms by their Septuagint numbering (e.g., Psalm 1 as 'the first voice of David'). Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and Hebrew Psalm numbering where applicable (e.g., Psalm 1). His quotations include Psalm 1:1, Exodus 20:13, and 1 Corinthians 8:4 and 10:20-21.
uncertain: The exact date of composition; it is placed in Tertullian's early Catholic period, likely between 197 and 202 AD, but cannot be fixed precisely.
The identity of the 'suauiludii' defender mentioned in section 20; the text is corrupt and the person is unnamed.
The reading of several corrupt passages in the Latin text, including the phrase about 'angeli' in section 2 and the description of the obelisk in section 8.
Whether Tertullian wrote this work before or after his 'Apology'; the relative chronology is debated.
The precise meaning of some technical terms related to the circus and theater, such as 'tensa', 'armamaxa', and 'dissignator', which are rendered from context.
The reference to 'Elian' in section 23 ('quem curru rapiendum diabolus aduersus Elian exornauit'); the text is a crux and may not refer to the biblical Elijah, or may be corrupt.
The identity of the goddess 'Messias' in section 8; the name is associated with harvests but is otherwise obscure.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He first answers pagan objections that pleasures do not offend God, then turns to Christians who claim Scripture does not explicitly forbid such entertainments.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: hac conscientia instructi aduersus opinionem ethnicorum conuertamur magis ad nostrorum detractatus. quorundam enim fides aut simplicior aut scrupulosior ad hanc abdicationem spectaculorum de scripturis auctoritatem exposcit
_unresolved_facts.fix: Tertullian first answers pagan objections (sections 1-2), then turns to Christians who seek scriptural authority for abstaining from shows (section 3). However, the brief's phrasing 'claim Scripture does not explicitly forbid' overstates the passive construction; the Christians 'exposcit' (demand/require) scriptural authority, not merely claim absence of explicit prohibition.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He traces the origins, titles, apparatus, places, and arts of the games to pagan gods and demon worship.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Tertullian traces origins, titles, apparatus, places, and arts to idolatry and demons, but 'demon worship' is too strong. The demons are said to operate through and delight in the shows (section 10: 'nequam spiritus scilicet, daemones'), but the primary framework is idolatry (idololatria), not active demon worship by participants.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections 20-24: 'He refutes the excuse that God sees all things without being defiled'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: sol, inquit, immo ipse etiam deus de caelo spectat nec contaminatur. sane, sol et in cloacam radios suos defert nec inquinatur.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'suauiludii' defender in section 20 compares the sun (and by extension God) watching from heaven without being defiled, not 'God sees all things without being defiled' as a general excuse. The brief misrepresents the specific analogy; it's about the sun/God's remote observation, not omniscience generally.

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections 25-27: 'He warns that no one can serve both God and the devil'
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'no one can serve two masters' saying appears in section 26, not 25-27 as a thematic heading. Section 25 focuses on the impossibility of mixing Christian worship with spectacle attendance; section 26 gives the demon examples and the two masters saying; section 27 focuses on blasphemy and persecution. The brief's thematic label is slightly misplaced.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Piso: 'Roman historian cited on the Tarpeian and Capitoline games.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: post hunc Numa Pompilius Marti et Robigini fecit... dehinc Tullus Hostilius, dehinc Ancus Martius et ceteri. qui quos quem per ordinem et quibus idolis ludos instituerint, positum est apud Suetonium Tranquillum uel a quibus Tranquillus accepit. sed haec satis erunt ad originis de idololatria reatum.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Piso is cited only for the Tarpeian games being called Capitolini: 'quos Tarpeios dictos et Capitolinos Piso tradit' (section 5). The brief correctly states this but the source text shows Piso is not cited for 'Capitoline games' as a separate institution but for the naming of Romulus's games to Jupiter Feretrius.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: quid enim, inquis, si alio in tempore circum adiero, periclitabor de inquinamento?
_unresolved_facts.fix: Section 8 contains a Christian interlocutor's question ('inquis'), not pagan objectors. The voice asks about entering the circus at another time and being polluted; this is an internal Christian question, not a pagan objection. The brief misidentifies the speaker.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Those who flatter themselves that no specific prohibition exists: 'sections: ["20"]'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Quam uana igitur, immo desperata argumentatio eorum, qui sine dubio tergiuersatione amittendae uoluptatis optendunt nullam eius abstinentiae mentionem specialiter uel localiter in scripturis determinari
_unresolved_facts.fix: This voice appears in section 20, but the brief's section reference for 'sibi blandiumtur' is wrong. The phrase 'sibi blandiumtur' appears in section 14: 'propter eos maxime qui sibi blandiumtur quod non nominatim abstinentia ista praescripta sit.' The brief conflates two different discussions: section 14 introduces those who flatter themselves, while section 20 introduces a new defense ('suauiludii').

_unresolved_facts.claim: Unattributed Gospel allusion: 'Introduced with 'inquit' but not explicitly identified as the Lord; likely an allusion to John 16:20'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: saeculum, inquit, gaudebit, uos tristes eritis.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The quotation in section 28 is introduced with 'inquit' but is explicitly attributed: 'saeculum, inquit, gaudebit, uos tristes eritis.' The 'inquit' refers to the Lord's saying in John 16:20, but Tertullian presents it as a general scriptural saying without explicit 'Lord' attribution. However, the brief's claim it's 'not explicitly identified as the Lord' is technically correct but 'likely an allusion to John 16:20' is speculative; Tertullian may be quoting from memory without precise attribution. The brief's 'unattributed Gospel allusion' framing is acceptable but the 'inquit' does not mark a voice in the same way as others.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: columnae Sessias a sementationibus, Messias a messibus, Tutulinas a tutela fructuum sustinent
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief renders 'Messias' as 'Messia' but the source has 'Messias' as a goddess name (nominative would be 'Messia' or 'Messias'). The brief's parenthetical '(associated with harvests)' is correct but the name form should be 'Messias' matching the source, or 'Messia' if normalized. The source form is 'Messias' in the Latin.

Tertullian says 'eosdem Samothracas existimant' referring to the 'Magnis Potentibus Valentibus' being identified as Samothracan gods. The brief adds '(the Great Gods)' which is interpretive; Tertullian does not use this title here, though 'Magni Dei' is a known epithet. The brief's gloss is not directly supported by this text.

Tertullian cites 'non occides' in section 2, but does not identify this as Exodus 20:13 or the Decalogue. The brief's attribution is anachronistic editorial identification, not Tertullian's own citation formula. This is a minor issue but the brief presents it as Tertullian's quotation practice.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The reference to 'Elian' in section 23 ('quem curru rapiendum diabolus aduersus Elian exornauit'); the text is a crux and may not refer to the biblical Elijah, or may be corrupt.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: quem curru rapiendum diabolus aduersus Elian exornauit
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief's uncertainty note is itself uncertain. 'Elian' is almost certainly the biblical Elijah (Elias in Latin, accusative Elian), given the chariot of fire reference in 2 Kings 2. The 'crux' is not whether it refers to Elijah but whether the text is corrupt in other ways (the chariot being prepared 'against' Elijah rather than for him). The brief overstates the uncertainty.
